passage.title: 'A Storm, Then Peace', a teacher-written review for TGA
paras: The Tempest begins with a shipwreck and ends with a pardon. In between, an exiled duke gathers his enemies on a magic island and must decide what to do with them.

It is the ending that makes the play extraordinary. Prospero could destroy those who ruined him; instead he forgives them. Shakespeare gives him a line that still feels brave: 'The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.'

Not every thread is tied. Antonio barely speaks, and Caliban's future is uncertain. Yet this honesty is a strength: forgiveness here is a choice, not a fairy tale. Four centuries on, it remains a play worth arguing about.

panels.title: How the reviewer persuades
points: Short summary first: no long plot retelling
Admits weaknesses, then turns them into strengths

judge the value or quality of something

questions.q: Find two evaluative adjectives and explain what they show.
questions.a: 'extraordinary' and 'brave': the reviewer admires the ending and Prospero's choice.

questions.q: How does the reviewer turn a weakness into a strength?
questions.a: Untied threads are called 'honesty': forgiveness is shown as a real choice, not a fairy tale.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a review paragraph about one scene of The Tempest. Summarise in one sentence, then evaluate with evidence. Starter: 'In Act...'
questions.a: One sentence of summary, evaluative adjectives, a short quotation and a clear judgement.

questions.q: Extend: add one weakness and turn it into a strength.
questions.a: For example: The exposition is long; however, it makes the later forgiveness more powerful.

questions.q: Stretch: give the play a star rating out of five and justify it in one sentence.
